markdown: AI Product Engineer RoadmapFrom "built a few tutorials" → job-ready remote startup engineer in 3–4 months (10–20hrs/week)This guide is built around one job: AI Product Engineer. Not ML researcher, not the person ﬁne-tuningfoundation models — the person who takes LLMs and turns them into shipped, reliable products. Startupsdon't hire this role for theory; they hire it because someone can open a codebase, understand an agentframework, and ship a feature by Friday. So this guide is organized to get you contributing to real repos (likeMastra, assistant-ui, mcp-use) as fast as possible, not to make you complete in isolation before touchingcode.How to use this: Each phase has a "build" deliverable. Do not move to the next phase until you've shippedthat thing, even badly. Depth comes from shipping and hitting real bugs, not from reading more.The mental map: what an AI Product Engineer actually needs to knowFive layers, roughly in order of how often you'll touch them:LLM API fundamentals — how you actually talk to models (structured outputs, streaming, function calling,cost/latency tradeoffs)Context engineering — RAG, retrieval, prompt design, managing what goes into the context window (this is80% of real AI product work)Agents & orchestration — tool use, multi-step reasoning, agent frameworks, memory, MCPApplication engineering — the "boring" backend/frontend skills that make it a product instead of anotebook: auth, streaming UIs, observability, evals, deploymentSystems thinking — reliability, cost control, latency, guardrails, when NOT to use an LLMResearch-track engineers go deep on layer 0 (model internals, training, ﬁne-tuning). You're explicitly skippingthat — you need just enough of it to reason about model behavior, not to build it.Phase 0 (Week 1): Foundations you're probably missingSince you've done tutorials but are still "beginner," spend one focused week ﬁlling gaps rather than re-learning what you know.

How transformers/LLMs work at a conceptual level — not the math, but: tokens, context windows,temperature/top-p, why hallucination happens, why models are bad at counting/arithmetic, what "attention"buys you intuitively. (Andrej Karpathy's "Intro to LLMs" video is the single best hour you can spend here.)The API surface of the major providers: Anthropic Messages API, OpenAI Responses/Chat CompletionsAPI. Learn: system prompts, multi-turn message arrays, streaming, tool/function calling schemas, structuredoutput (JSON mode/tool-forced output), vision input.Local dev setup: Python venv + uv (fast, increasingly standard), and since your OSS targets are TypeScript-heavy (Mastra, assistant-ui), get comfortable with Node/TS tooling too — pnpm, tsx, basic async/awaitpatterns in TS.Build: A CLI tool that calls an LLM API with streaming output and one tool call (e.g., a weather or calculatortool). Do it once in Python, once in TypeScript. This dual-stack ﬂuency matters a lot for your OSS targets.Phase 1 (Weeks 2–4): Context engineering — RAG done properlyMost " AI isn't working" bug reports in real products are context problems, not model problems. This is thehighest-leverage skill you can have.Topics:Chunking strategies (ﬁxed-size vs. semantic vs. recursive) and why chunk boundaries silently wreck retrievalqualityEmbeddings: what they are, cosine similarity, when embeddings fail (they're bad at exact keyword/numericmatching — this is why hybrid search exists)Vector databases: pick ONE to go deep on (pgvector if you want to stay Postgres-native and hireable, orChroma/Qdrant for a dedicated vector store) — don't survey ﬁve shallowlyHybrid search (BM25/keyword + vector) and re-ranking (cross-encoders, Cohere rerank)Query transformation: query expansion, HyDE, multi-query retrievalChunking + retrieval evaluation: how do you know your RAG pipeline is actually good? (recall@k, answerrelevance)Long-context vs. RAG tradeoffs — increasingly models have huge context windows; know when to just stuffcontext vs. when retrieval still wins (cost, latency, needle-in-haystack degradation)Build: RAG-over-your-own-docs app (e.g., chat with a PDF/codebase). Then deliberately break it — feed it adocument type it handles badly, measure why, ﬁx it. This debugging loop is the actual skill.Phase 2 (Weeks 4–7): Agents, tool use & MCPThis is where you connect directly to your OSS strategy — Mastra and mcp-use are agent/MCP-nativeframeworks.Topics:

To o l / fu n c t i o n  c a l l i n g  i n  d e pt h :  s c h e m a  d e s i g n ,  p a ra l l e l  to o l  c a l l s ,  e r r o r  h a n d l i n g  w h e n  t h e  m o d e l  c a l l s  a  to o lwrongAgent loop patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, reﬂection loopsModel Context Protocol (MCP) — this is becoming the standard for tool/context interoperability;understand it well enough to build both an MCP server and consume one as a client. Directly relevant to mcp-use.Agent frameworks — go deep on one, be conversationally competent in others:Mastra (TypeScript, since it's one of your targets) — workﬂows, agents, memory primitivesLangGraph / LangChain (Python, still the most widely-referenced in job postings)Vercel AI SDK (TS, very relevant since it pairs with assistant-ui)Memory in agents: short-term (conversation buffer) vs. long-term (vector-backed memory, summarizationstrategies)Multi-agent patterns: when orchestrating multiple agents actually helps vs. adds pointless complexity(usually it adds complexity — know the tradeoff)Computer-use / browser-use agents at a conceptual level, since Cua is in your target list — how screen-basedagents differ from API-tool agentsBuild: An agent with 3+ real tools (not toy ones — e.g., search + a database write + an external API) that canchain them to complete a multi-step task. Then wrap it as an MCP server so another client could use it.Phase 3 (Weeks 7–10): Application engineering — making it a productThis is the layer most " AI tutorial" learners skip, and it's exactly what separates a demo from something astartup will pay you to build.Topics:

Streaming UIs: server-sent events / streaming responses to the frontend, optimistic UI updates, handlingpartial/malformed streamed JSONassistant-ui (your OSS target) and Vercel AI SDK's useChat/useCompletion — the standard patterns forbuilding chat UIs in ReactStructured output reliability: JSON schema validation, retry-on-malformed-output patterns, Zod (TS) /Pydantic (Python) for validating LLM output before it touches your app logicEvals: this is the single most underrated skill in AI product engineering. Learn to write eval sets (even 20-50examples), use an LLM-as-judge pattern, track regressions when you change a prompt. Without evals you'reﬂying blind on every prompt change.Observability: tracing LLM calls (LangSmith, Langfuse, or just structured logging), tracking token usage/cost/latency per requestGuardrails: input validation, output ﬁltering, prompt injection basics (know what it is and the standardmitigations even though it's not fully solvable)Auth + multi-tenancy basics: most startup product work assumes you can bolt AI features onto a normalSaaS app — don't neglect this because it's "not AI"Deployment: containerizing a Python/Node AI service, environment/secrets management, basic rate limitingand queueing for expensive LLM callsBuild: T ake your Phase 2 agent and put a real streaming chat UI on it using assistant-ui or the Vercel AI SDK,add structured output validation, and write a 20-case eval suite for it. This is close to a portfolio-readyproject.Phase 4 (Weeks 10–14): Systems thinking, cost/latency, and portfoliopolishTopics:Cost modeling: per-request token cost math, when to use a smaller/cheaper model vs. a frontier model,prompt caching (Anthropic/OpenAI both support this — big cost lever)Latency optimization: streaming-ﬁrst UX, speculative/parallel tool calls, when to precompute vs. compute on-demandModel routing: using a cheap model to classify/route and an expensive model only when neededFine-tuning vs. prompting vs. RAG — know the decision tree even if you never ﬁne-tune yourself (you'll beasked about it in interviews)Security basics speciﬁc to AI products: prompt injection via retrieved documents/tool outputs, data leakagethrough prompts/logsBuild/polish:Turn your best 1-2 projects into genuinely polished, documented, deployed portfolio pieces (live demo link,not just a repo)This is also the point to fold in your existing OSS strategy — the skills from Phases 1-3 are exactly what youneed to make a real, useful contribution to Mastra/assistant-ui/mcp-use/Cua rather than a drive-by typo PR

Suggested weekly rhythm (10-20 hrs/week)40% building your current phase's project30% reading source code of your target OSS repos (this doubles as job-search prep)20% structured learning (docs, one long-form course/video, papers-if-relevant — skip deep research papersunless directly useful)10% writing up what you learned (even just notes) — this becomes interview material and blog content laterWhat to deliberately skip (research-track topics, not your job)Pretraining/ﬁne-tuning models from scratch, distributed training infraDeep transformer math / attention mechanism derivations beyond intuitionNovel architecture research (mixture-of-experts internals, etc.)RLHF/RLAIF implementation detailsYo u  n e e d  to  understand these exist and roughly what they do (interviewers will probe general literacy), butbuilding expertise here isn't the job you're going for.How this maps to your job searchGiven your target repos:Mastra → Phase 2 (agents/TS) is your direct prep groundassistant-ui → Phase 3 (streaming UIs, chat UX) is your direct prep groundmcp-use → Phase 2's MCP section is your direct prep groundCua → Phase 2's computer-use section + Phase 3's guardrails/securityBy week 7-8 you should already be capable of reading and contributing small ﬁxes to these repos; by week10-14 you should be able to ship a real feature, which is exactly the "heavy OSS contribution" lever youroutreach strategy depends on.
